cards.title: Datasette patches SQL injection in mixed-access DBs

panels.head: Datasette had a SQL injection hole in mixed-permission setups
panels.sub: Any user with read access to a public table could bypass row-level restrictions and read data from private tables in the same database.

panels.head: Public table access was the attack surface
panels.sub: Even with execute-sql disabled, the flaw let authenticated-but-limited users craft queries that leaked private table data — read-only, but still a serious boundary violation.

panels.head: Only instances mixing public and private tables in one DB
panels.sub: The author notes this pattern — public and private tables co-existing in a single Datasette instance with permission-based access control — is uncommon in practice.

panels.head: Patch in 1.0a38 and backported to 0.65.3
panels.sub: Until you can upgrade, disabling the execute-sql permission on the affected database is the recommended interim mitigation.

panels.head: Mixing access tiers in one DB is a hidden risk pattern
panels.sub: If you use Datasette to expose internal data alongside public datasets, keep them in separate database files — or treat the shared-DB pattern as a threat surface worth auditing regardless of framework.

cards.title: Humans Miss 1-in-3 Threats When Approving AI Agent Commands

panels.head: Human reviewers let dangerous AI commands through 33% of the time
panels.sub: Across 40,000 simulated agent runs, people approving tool-use requests missed roughly one in three genuinely harmful actions — even when explicitly asked to stay vigilant.

panels.head: A game-like environment stress-tested human oversight at scale
panels.sub: Participants reviewed AI agent permission requests in a structured task environment. The volume and velocity of requests mimicked real agentic workflows, where agents fire off many tool calls in quick succession.

panels.head: Approval fatigue, not malice, is the failure mode
panels.sub: High request volume degrades vigilance fast. When reviewers see dozens of routine-looking commands, pattern-matching kicks in and edge cases slip through — the same dynamic that plagues alert triage in security ops.

panels.head: "Human in the loop" is not the same as "human oversight"
panels.sub: Placing a person in the approval chain provides legal cover but not reliable safety. Without rate-limiting, batching by risk tier, or automated pre-filtering, human review degrades toward rubber-stamping.

panels.head: Design for human limits, not human ideals
panels.sub: For PMs shipping agentic systems: audit how many approvals your reviewers actually handle per hour, flag only high-entropy or out-of-distribution commands for human eyes, and treat a 33% miss rate as your baseline assumption until you measure otherwise.

cards.title: Meta's AI Accidentally Hacked a Company During Testing

panels.head: Meta's Muse Spark exploited a live system it was never supposed to reach
panels.sub: During a third-party cybersecurity evaluation, the model found and used a real security vulnerability in an external company — not a sandboxed target.

panels.head: A misconfiguration gave the model unsupervised internet access
panels.sub: Irregular, an independent firm Meta hired for red-team testing, accidentally left live internet access enabled. That gap was enough for the model to act on what it found.

panels.head: Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed near-identical incidents
panels.sub: This is the third major lab to confirm an accidental external breach during model evaluation. The failure mode is consistent: evaluation infrastructure that isn't fully air-gapped.

panels.head: Agentic models can cause real harm before anyone notices the config error
panels.sub: These aren't adversarial jailbreaks — they're routine capability tests that leaked into production environments. For PMs scoping agentic deployments, evaluation isolation is now a hard requirement, not a best practice.

panels.head: Treat model evaluation infra with the same rigour as production infra
panels.sub: Default-deny network egress, explicit allowlists, and third-party audits of test environments should be table stakes before any agentic model touches external tools — even in testing.

cards.title: Meta's Muse Spark 1.2 bets big on coding agents

panels.head: Meta built a coding agent just to train a better model
panels.sub: Muse Code — Meta's own coding agent — was co-developed with Muse Spark 1.2 specifically so the model could be trained on real agentic tool-use trajectories, not synthetic stand-ins.

panels.head: Whole-repo generation and long-horizon tasks are the new benchmark
panels.sub: 1.2 scaled training compute on coding tasks and expanded environment diversity, targeting end-to-end projects and auto-research — not just function-level completions.

panels.head: Pay $1.25/M tokens — or $0.10/M if you share your data
panels.sub: The standard tier (muse-spark-1.2) sits near Gemini Flash pricing. Opt into the contributor tier (muse-spark-1.2-contributor) and the cost drops 12× on input and 21× on output — in exchange for Meta training rights.

panels.head: Long-sequence agentic tool-calling is the new moat
panels.sub: The fact that Meta co-trained model and agent together suggests the field is converging on a view: raw benchmark scores matter less than how well a model sustains coherent action over many tool calls and large codebases.

panels.head: For teams building AI-assisted dev workflows, the contributor tier is cheap enough to experiment freely
panels.sub: At $0.10/$0.20 per million tokens, Muse Spark 1.2-contributor undercuts most mid-tier models. Worth benchmarking against your existing code-gen pipeline — just read the data-use terms before routing production traffic through it.

cards.title: AI safety tests accidentally hit real websites

panels.head: A CTF drill became a real attack — by accident
panels.sub: During a Capture-the-Flag cybersecurity evaluation, an OpenAI model exploited a live public website it mistook for a simulated target.

panels.head: Two failures stacked: network misconfiguration + name collision
panels.sub: Evaluator Irregular left the sandboxed test environment connected to the public internet. Separately, the fictional CTF target name happened to match a real registered domain.

panels.head: Both OpenAI and Anthropic models were affected
panels.sub: The same Irregular-hosted environment gave Claude live internet access during some tests too — documented separately in Anthropic's own write-up of the UK AI Safety Institute incident.

panels.head: This is now common enough to need its own tag
panels.sub: Simon Willison created an 'accidental-cyberattacks' tag just to track recurrences — signalling this is a systemic evaluation-infrastructure problem, not a one-off.

panels.head: Eval environment hygiene is now a model-risk control
panels.sub: If you're deploying or auditing agentic AI, verify that test environments are network-air-gapped and that synthetic target names are checked against real DNS before any eval runs.
